translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“It speaks of flourishing virtue and the highest good, which the people cannot forget.”

Wang Cheng 王珵

Comment by Associate Examiner Fang, Instructor: “This topic from the Great Learning is supremely dignified. Candidates in the examination hall have failed to grasp it truly and have mostly followed familiar precedents. This essay apprehends principle with precision and depth; its vigor is abundant and its expression rich, without a single stale phrase. It should be recorded as a model for later students.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor: “The commentary and annotations are clear enough in themselves, yet most writers are tiresomely verbose and vague. This essay alone is closely attuned to the subject and rich in meaning, without a single superfluous phrase. Its author must be deeply versed in the learning of principle.”

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Instructor: “Its language follows principle, and its elucidation is penetrating and thorough. Among a thousand essays cast in the same mold, this is the sole such script we have found. It should promptly be committed to the printing blocks.”

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Instructor: “The substance of manifesting luminous virtue and resting in the highest good requires just such an expression of admiration to do it justice.”

In explaining the poem, the author of the commentary speaks of the utmost attainment of the gentleman and the depth of his influence upon others. For flourishing virtue and the highest good are what all human hearts alike recognize as right. Once the gentleman has attained them before others, surely his power to move the people so that they never forget him is something that cannot of itself be restrained! title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
澳之詩明明德者之止於至善此則指其實而
歎美之謂夫不易感者民心不可誣者明德詩
云有斐君子終不可諠兮者豈無謂耶盖言明
明德之君子一身所萃有以充此心之全體渾
然萬理之畢具何有於滲漏一已所得有以妙
此心之大用沛然萬事之順應何有於假借游
泳於物則至精至當之地纖瑕莫指一人道之
標準也陟降於民彜無頗無僻之鄉一疵不存
一人倫之表極也閎於中肆於外可法而可則
===
根於心生於色可觀而可度夫君子備是盛德
至善如此顧何心於民之不忘哉殆見民雖不
同而所同者此心拭目乎盛德之光範自有以
啓其景仰之懷心雖不同而所同者此理濡耳
乎至善之休風自有以動其企慕之念一家仰
之不忘一國仰之不忘巍乎山斗之在上而在
在具瞻也一國慕之不忘天下慕之不忘儼乎
麟鳳之瑞世而人人快覩也是非不欲忘也懿
德之在人心天理自孚殆有繋於衷而不能已
punctuated: 澳之詩，明明德者之止於至善，此則指其實而歎美之。謂夫不易感者民心，不可誣者明德。詩云：「有斐君子，終不可諠兮。」者，豈無謂耶？盖言明明德之君子，一身所萃，有以充此心之全體，渾然萬理之畢具，何有於滲漏？一已所得，有以妙此心之大用，沛然萬事之順應，何有於假借？游泳於物則至精至當之地，纖瑕莫指，一人道之標準也；陟降於民彜無頗無僻之鄉，一疵不存，一人倫之表極也。閎於中，肆於外，可法而可則；根於心，生於色，可觀而可度。夫君子備是盛德至善如此，顧何心於民之不忘哉？殆見民雖不同，而所同者此心，拭目乎盛德之光範，自有以啓其景仰之懷；心雖不同，而所同者此理，濡耳乎至善之休風，自有以動其企慕之念。一家仰之不忘，一國仰之不忘，巍乎山斗之在上，而在在具瞻也；一國慕之不忘，天下慕之不忘，儼乎麟鳳之瑞世，而人人快覩也。是非不欲忘也，懿德之在人心，天理自孚，殆有繋於衷而不能已
translation_en: …the poem “The Banks of the Qi” to illuminate how those who make bright their bright virtue come to rest in the highest good; here it points to the substance of their achievement and praises it with admiration. Now, the people’s hearts are not easily moved, and bright virtue cannot be counterfeited. The Book of Odes says, “That cultivated gentleman can never be forgotten.” Could these words be without meaning? They mean that the gentleman who makes bright his bright virtue gathers within himself what fills out the entire substance of this heart. All principles are fully present in an undivided whole: how could there be any omission? What he has attained within himself brings the great functioning of this heart to perfection. It responds abundantly and appropriately to every affair: how could there be anything borrowed or contrived? He moves freely within the utmost refinement and fittingness of the norms inherent in things. Not the slightest flaw can be pointed out: he is a standard for human conduct. In all his movements he remains within the constant norms of human life, without partiality or deviation. Not a single blemish remains: he is a supreme model for human relationships. Expansive within and fully manifest without, his virtue can serve as a model and a rule; rooted in his heart and appearing in his countenance, it can be observed and taken as a measure. Possessing such abundant virtue and highest goodness, what concern could the gentleman have for whether the people forget him? We see that although people differ, they share this same heart. When they clear their eyes to behold the radiant example of abundant virtue, it naturally awakens their reverence. Although their hearts differ, they share this same principle. When their ears are steeped in the beneficent influence of the highest good, it naturally stirs their longing to emulate him. A household looks up to him and does not forget; a state looks up to him and does not forget. Lofty above them like Mount Tai and the Northern Dipper, he is gazed upon everywhere. A state admires him and does not forget; all under Heaven admire him and do not forget. Majestic like the qilin and phoenix bringing auspicious signs to the world, he delights everyone who beholds him. This is not simply a matter of being unwilling to forget. When splendid virtue dwells in people’s hearts, heavenly principle naturally wins their trust; something binds them inwardly, and they cannot cease…

title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
者私媚云乎哉是非不敢忘也理義之悅人心
天機自動卒有纓於情而不容巳者驩虞云乎
哉是則君子極所得於己而深所仰於人如此
傳者釋詩以明明明德者之止至善不其至乎
抑淇澳之詩衞人所以美武公者大學乃引之
以明明德者之止至善豈古聖之可法獨一武
公歟要之此詩首言求止之方次言得止之驗
終言得止之實功不缺而序不紊足以示學者
入德之門造道之的故引之耳然推其極雖堯
===
之克明湯之懋昭亦不外此學者誠知加求止
之功循求止之序則盛德至善在我武公二聖
之地位可至而文武親賢樂利之業又不過舉
此措之耳先儒謂先引淇澳明明德者之得所
止所以發新民之端後引烈文明新民之得所
止所以著明明德之驗詎不信夫
知者動仁者靜
方策
同考試官訓導鄭 批 論語題士子每發
punctuated:
者，私媚云乎哉？是非不敢忘也，理義之悅人心，天機自動，卒有纓於情而不容巳者，驩虞云乎哉？是則君子極所得於己，而深所仰於人如此。傳者釋詩，以明明明德者之止至善，不其至乎？抑《淇澳》之詩，衞人所以美武公者，《大學》乃引之以明明德者之止至善，豈古聖之可法，獨一武公歟？要之，此詩首言求止之方，次言得止之驗，終言得止之實，功不缺而序不紊，足以示學者入德之門、造道之的，故引之耳。然推其極，雖堯之克明、湯之懋昭，亦不外此。學者誠知加求止之功，循求止之序，則盛德至善在我，武公、二聖之地位可至，而文武親賢樂利之業，又不過舉此措之耳。先儒謂先引《淇澳》，明明德者之得所止，所以發新民之端；後引《烈文》，明新民之得所止，所以著明明德之驗。詎不信夫！
知者動，仁者靜。
方策
同考試官訓導鄭批：《論語》題，士子每發
translation_en:
…such feelings cannot be restrained. Could this be called self-interested flattery? It is not that the people dare not forget: principle and righteousness delight the human heart, and its innate workings stir of themselves, ultimately becoming bound up with feelings that cannot be checked. Could this be called mere enjoyment and pleasure? Thus the gentleman brings his own attainment to its utmost and inspires profound admiration in others. The author of the commentary explains the poem to illuminate how those who manifest luminous virtue come to rest in the highest good. Is this not an exposition of the utmost completeness?
Yet “The Bend of the Qi” (Qi ao) is a poem in which the people of Wei praised Duke Wu. The Great Learning cites it to explain how those who manifest luminous virtue come to rest in the highest good. Could Duke Wu alone, among the ancient sages, be worthy of emulation? The essential point is that this poem first describes the method of seeking that resting place, next the evidence of having attained it, and finally the substance of that attainment. No part of the effort is missing, and its sequence is not confused. It suffices to show learners the gateway into virtue and the goal of advancing in the Way; that is why it is cited. Pushed to its fullest extent, even Yao’s capacity to manifest virtue and Tang’s diligent illumination of it do not go beyond this. If learners truly know to apply themselves to seeking this resting place and to follow the proper sequence in seeking it, then abundant virtue and the highest good will be within themselves, and the standing of Duke Wu and the two sages can be attained. Even the achievements of Kings Wen and Wu—through which people cherished their kin, honored the worthy, enjoyed their pleasures, and benefited from their benefits—amount to no more than putting this into practice. Earlier Confucian scholars said that “The Bend of the Qi” is cited first to explain how those who manifest luminous virtue attain their proper resting place, thereby introducing the renewal of the people; “Illustrious” (Lie wen) is cited afterward to explain how renewing the people attains its proper resting place, thereby displaying the evidence of manifesting luminous virtue. Is this not indeed true?
“The wise are active; the benevolent are still.”
Fang Ce

title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
動靜二字不出令人厭觀此篇融會傳註成文
且挑剔明白而知仁體段宛然在目必嘗苦心
於本領者
考試官教諭姜批動靜字發揮痛快且
用字用句無一竒怪險僻讀之令人躍然録
之以式
考試官教諭張批題似平易而措辭實
難此作不為題窘其必富於學者
聖人論人之造理異而具體自異焉蓋理之在
===
人本同而人之所造則異也則夫體段之具又
得無一動一靜之異哉聖人各著以示人宜矣
且夫欲知知仁之喜好不同當知知仁之體段
本異是故知周明通而是非昭然其不昧知者
也知者之體主於動動豈蕩無所見而徇物哉
想其一事具一理也此心有以達其幾微萬事
具萬理也此心有以達其妙用接於日用者有
常有變而應之在我者無適無莫隨宜制事不
拘於一隅也散之天下者有順有逆而處之在
punctuated:
動靜二字不出，令人厭觀。此篇融會傳註成文，且挑剔明白，而知仁體段宛然在目，必嘗苦心於本領者。
考試官教諭姜批：動靜字發揮痛快，且用字用句無一竒怪險僻，讀之令人躍然，録之以式。
考試官教諭張批：題似平易，而措辭實難。此作不為題窘，其必富於學者。
聖人論人之造理異，而具體自異焉。蓋理之在人本同，而人之所造則異也，則夫體段之具，又得無一動一靜之異哉？聖人各著以示人，宜矣。且夫欲知知仁之喜好不同，當知知仁之體段本異。是故知周明通，而是非昭然，其不昧，知者也。知者之體主於動，動豈蕩無所見而徇物哉？想其一事具一理也，此心有以達其幾微；萬事具萬理也，此心有以達其妙用。接於日用者有常有變，而應之在我者無適無莫，隨宜制事，不拘於一隅也；散之天下者有順有逆，而處之在
translation_en:
…fail to bring out the meaning of the two words “activity” and “stillness,” making their work tiresome to read. This essay integrates the commentaries into its composition and draws distinctions clearly, so that the characteristic dispositions of wisdom and benevolence stand vividly before the reader’s eyes. Its author must have devoted painstaking effort to the fundamentals.
Examiner Jiang, Instructor, comments: The words “activity” and “stillness” are expounded with satisfying force and clarity. Moreover, neither the wording nor the phrasing is at all strange, strained, or obscure. Reading it lifts the spirits. It is recorded here to serve as a model.
Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: The topic seems straightforward, yet expressing it is truly difficult. This composition is not constrained by the topic; its author must possess extensive learning.
The Sage discusses how people differ in their attainment of principle, and how their characteristic dispositions naturally differ accordingly. For principle is fundamentally the same in everyone, but people differ in what they attain. How, then, could their dispositions fail to differ, one being active and another still? It is fitting that the Sage should make each manifest to instruct others. Moreover, if we wish to understand why the wise and the benevolent differ in what they delight in, we must understand that their characteristic dispositions are fundamentally different. Thus, one whose understanding is comprehensive, clear, and penetrating, to whom right and wrong are plainly apparent and never obscured, is wise. The disposition of the wise centers on activity. But could such activity mean drifting without discernment and submitting to external things? Consider: each affair embodies a principle, and this mind can apprehend its subtle incipience; the myriad affairs embody myriad principles, and this mind can apprehend their wondrous workings. What we encounter in daily life includes both the constant and the changing, while in responding we neither insist upon nor reject any course in advance. We manage affairs as circumstances require, without being confined to a single standpoint. Throughout the world there are both favorable and adverse circumstances, while the handling of them rests in…

title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
我者無將無迎因時順理不泥於一端也左之
左之旁取逢原之有資右之右之泛應曲當之
無礙動非此之謂乎欲淨理還而心德渾然其
克全仁者也仁者之體主於靜靜豈寂無所感
而絶物哉想其處物為義也彼則安于此而依
之深在物為理也彼則安于此而守之固物之
常變叢於前而吾心之敦厚一義自持無歆羨
也境之順逆變於前而吾心之凝重一理自定
無畔援也肫肫乎自暫至久不因物而有遷坦
===
坦乎由少而老不知誘而物化靜非此之謂乎
是則知者未嘗不靜而其體則主於動仁者未
嘗不動而其體則主於靜此所以其樂有山水
而其效有樂壽也歟抑嘗因是言而求其人若
賜之達而優於從政即知者之動若顏之愚而
三月不違即仁者之靜至吾夫子則合斯二者
而兼全之觀其設教杏壇因材變化何如其知
動厄於陳蔡絃歌自如何如其仁靜要之夫子
一身太極之全體也先儒謂其非體仁知之深
punctuated:
我者，無將無迎，因時順理，不泥於一端也。左之左之，旁取逢原之有資；右之右之，泛應曲當之無礙。動非此之謂乎？欲淨理還，而心德渾然其克全，仁者也。仁者之體主於靜，靜豈寂無所感而絶物哉？想其處物為義也，彼則安于此而依之深；在物為理也，彼則安于此而守之固。物之常變叢於前，而吾心之敦厚，一義自持，無歆羨也；境之順逆變於前，而吾心之凝重，一理自定，無畔援也。肫肫乎，自暫至久，不因物而有遷；坦坦乎，由少而老，不知誘而物化。靜非此之謂乎？
是則知者未嘗不靜，而其體則主於動；仁者未嘗不動，而其體則主於靜。此所以其樂有山水，而其效有樂壽也歟？抑嘗因是言而求其人，若賜之達而優於從政，即知者之動；若顏之愚而三月不違，即仁者之靜。至吾夫子，則合斯二者而兼全之。觀其設教杏壇，因材變化，何如其知動！厄於陳蔡，絃歌自如，何如其仁靜！要之，夫子一身，太極之全體也。先儒謂其非體仁知之深
translation_en:
…on my part, neither sending things off nor anticipating their arrival, I follow the times and accord with principle, without clinging to any single course. Turning this way and that, one draws abundantly from the source wherever one reaches; turning here and there, one responds freely to everything, fitting each particular circumstance without obstruction. Is this not what is meant by activity? When desires are cleared away and principle restored, and the virtue of the mind is whole and complete, this is the benevolent person. The fundamental disposition of the benevolent centers on stillness. But could stillness mean being inert and unresponsive, cut off from things? Consider righteousness as the proper handling of things: the benevolent person rests securely in it and relies on it deeply. Consider principle as inherent in things: the benevolent person rests securely in it and holds to it firmly. Whether ordinary or changing circumstances crowd before me, my mind remains generous and steadfast, sustaining itself by righteousness alone, without longing or envy. Whether favorable or adverse conditions change before me, my mind remains composed and steady, settling itself by principle alone, without straying or grasping. Utterly sincere, from a brief interval to a long span, one does not shift with external things; entirely at ease, from youth to old age, one is not lured away or transformed by things. Is this not what is meant by stillness?
Thus the wise are never without stillness, yet their fundamental disposition centers on activity; the benevolent are never without activity, yet their fundamental disposition centers on stillness. Is this why they delight respectively in water and mountains, and why the resulting benefits are joy and longevity? I have also sought, through these words, the people who exemplify them. Ci's discernment and his excellence in conducting government exemplify the activity of the wise; Yan's apparent dullness and his not departing from benevolence for three months exemplify the stillness of the benevolent. Our Master, however, united both and possessed them fully. Observe how he taught at the Apricot Altar, transforming his pupils according to their abilities: how great was the activity of his wisdom! Beset by hardship in Chen and Cai, he continued playing the strings and singing with his customary ease: how great was the stillness of his benevolence! In essence, the Master embodied in his own person the complete substance of the Supreme Ultimate. An earlier Confucian scholar said that, without profoundly embodying benevolence and wisdom, he …

title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
不能如此形容旨哉言乎
聖人治天下使有菽粟如水火菽粟如水
火而民焉有不仁者乎
鄭琬
考試官教諭姜批題本不難作者多認
理不定詞率泛冗令人厭觀獨此篇明白切當
而且氣格舂容擺脫塵俗信非穉筆可到執
此可以知子之為政矣
考試官教諭張批塲中作孟子義佳者
絕少此篇信筆胷中寫出聖人治天下化民
成俗之由深得立言本意且才思英發詞
語精健必八桂瓌竒養之有素者也可嘉
可嘉
聖人治世惟有以足民食自有以興民行甚矣
民食治化之所關也聖人有道以足之則民行
之興亦自有不容已者乎想昔孟子之意謂夫
不患世未治而患民心之未仁不患民未仁而
患政制之未善是故聖人者出以一身而撫輿圖
punctuated:
不能如此形容。旨哉，言乎！

聖人治天下，使有菽粟如水火。菽粟如水火，而民焉有不仁者乎？

鄭琬

考試官教諭姜批：題本不難，作者多認理不定，詞率泛冗，令人厭觀。獨此篇明白切當，而且氣格舂容，擺脫塵俗，信非穉筆可到。執此可以知子之為政矣。

考試官教諭張批：塲中作孟子義佳者絕少，此篇信筆胷中寫出聖人治天下、化民成俗之由，深得立言本意。且才思英發，詞語精健，必八桂瓌竒養之有素者也。可嘉，可嘉！

聖人治世，惟有以足民食，自有以興民行。甚矣，民食治化之所關也！聖人有道以足之，則民行之興，亦自有不容已者乎！想昔孟子之意，謂夫不患世未治，而患民心之未仁；不患民未仁，而患政制之未善。是故聖人者出，以一身而撫輿圖
translation_en:
…could not have described them in this way. How profound these words are!

“When a sage governs All under Heaven, he ensures that beans and grain are as plentiful as water and fire. When beans and grain are as plentiful as water and fire, how could any of the people fail to be benevolent?”

Zheng Wan

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Instructor: The topic itself is not difficult, but most writers lack a firm grasp of its principle. Their language is generally vague and prolix, making it tiresome to read. This essay alone is clear and apt; moreover, its spirit and style are ample and composed, free of commonplace vulgarity. Such writing is certainly beyond an immature hand. From this one can discern how you would conduct government.

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Instructor: Among the essays on the meaning of the Mencius written in the examination hall, good ones are exceedingly rare. In this essay, the writer lets his brush freely express what is in his breast, explaining how a sage governs All under Heaven, transforms the people, and establishes good customs. It grasps deeply the original intent of the statement. Moreover, its thought is brilliant and its language vigorous and precise. The writer must surely be an extraordinary talent of Bagui, long nurtured and cultivated. Commendable, commendable!

When a sage governs the world, provided he has the means to ensure that the people have sufficient food, he naturally has the means to elevate their conduct. How profoundly the people’s sustenance bears upon government and moral transformation! If a sage has a way to provide them with enough, will not the improvement of their conduct also follow of itself, irresistibly? I imagine that Mencius’s meaning in former times was this: one should worry not that the world is still ungoverned, but that the people’s hearts are not yet benevolent; one should worry not that the people are not yet benevolent, but that governmental institutions are not yet good. Thus, when a sage comes forth, he takes it upon himself alone to care for the territory…

title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
之廣以一人而宰兆民之繁知治世當以大德
也于焉易田薄歛立善政以開民菽粟之源知
為政不在小惠也于焉食時用禮制成規以節
民菽粟之流使其藏於民者源源相繼比閭無
間於族黨如水火之時時常足隨取而隨與也
不云烝民其乃粒乎使其蓄於下者陳陳相因
鄉遂無間於都鄙如水火之在在皆給隨求而
隨得也不云百室其盈止乎夫菽粟如水火則
衣食足而禮義自生俯仰給而廉恥自作將見
===
民之出作入息者一皆興孝興弟篤恩義於綱
常倫理之天民之耕食鑿飲者罔不興禮興讓
惇良心於民彝物則之域仁風行而偷風消閭
閻之下殆有所謂順帝之則者矣求其胥戕而
不仁者何有乎仁俗洽而澆俗泯里巷之間殆
有所謂徧為爾德者矣求其胥殘而不仁者何
得乎吁以民行之興而由於民食之足如此有
天下者可不知所先務哉抑論之民生固不可
無養而民富則不可無教斯二者治天下之本
punctuated: 之廣，以一人而宰兆民之繁，知治世當以大德也，于焉易田薄歛，立善政以開民菽粟之源；知為政不在小惠也，于焉食時用禮，制成規以節民菽粟之流。使其藏於民者源源相繼，比閭無間於族黨，如水火之時時常足，隨取而隨與也，不云「烝民其乃粒」乎？使其蓄於下者陳陳相因，鄉遂無間於都鄙，如水火之在在皆給，隨求而隨得也，不云「百室其盈止」乎？夫菽粟如水火，則衣食足而禮義自生，俯仰給而廉恥自作。將見民之出作入息者，一皆興孝興弟，篤恩義於綱常倫理之天；民之耕食鑿飲者，罔不興禮興讓，惇良心於民彝物則之域。仁風行而偷風消，閭閻之下殆有所謂「順帝之則」者矣，求其胥戕而不仁者何有乎？仁俗洽而澆俗泯，里巷之間殆有所謂「徧為爾德」者矣，求其胥殘而不仁者何得乎？吁！以民行之興而由於民食之足如此，有天下者可不知所先務哉？抑論之，民生固不可無養，而民富則不可無教，斯二者治天下之本
translation_en:
…in its vast extent, and, as a single person, governs the teeming multitude. Knowing that ordering the world requires great virtue, the sage therefore ensures that fields are well cultivated and levies light, establishing good government to open up the sources of the people’s beans and grain. Knowing that government does not consist in petty favors, he therefore regulates eating according to the seasons and expenditure according to ritual, establishing standing rules to restrain the outflow of the people’s beans and grain. Thus the provisions stored among the people are continually replenished, without distinction between the smaller neighborhood groupings and the larger community units. Like water and fire, they are always sufficient: whenever someone seeks them, they are supplied. Is it not said, “The multitude were thereby fed with grain”? He ensures that the stocks accumulated among the common people build up, old stores upon old stores, without distinction between the rural districts and the towns and outlying settlements. Like water and fire, they are sufficient everywhere: whenever sought, they are obtained. Is it not said, “The hundred households are full”?

When beans and grain are as plentiful as water and fire, clothing and food suffice, and ritual propriety and righteousness arise of themselves; provision for parents above and dependents below is adequate, and integrity and a sense of shame awaken of themselves. We shall then see the people who go out to work and return home to rest all inspired to filial devotion and respect for elder brothers, deepening their affection and righteousness within the Heaven-ordained bonds and moral relationships. Those who till the soil for food and dig wells for drink will all be inspired to ritual propriety and deference, strengthening their innate moral sense within the realm of constant human norms and the principles governing things. Benevolent ways will prevail and lax ways disappear. Among ordinary households there will surely be what is called “following the Lord on High’s standards.” Where could one find anyone who cruelly harms others? Benevolent customs will spread everywhere and shallow customs vanish. In the lanes and alleys there will surely be what is called “all practicing your virtue.” Where could one find anyone who cruelly injures others?

Ah! Since the flourishing of the people’s conduct depends in this way upon the sufficiency of their food, can one who possesses All under Heaven fail to know which task must come first? Yet, to pursue the matter further, the people’s livelihood certainly cannot do without material support; and once the people are prosperous, they cannot do without instruction. These two are the foundations of governing All under Heaven…

title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
可偏廢也古帝王所以仁民之道率不外此然
論其施為之序則養民尤其急務况戰國之時
民窮財盡救死不贍奚暇治禮義哉故孟子於
此章之論獨歸重於養民之政是雖有所感而
發亦曰教由養立欲君人者先急其本而後驅
之善非謂民食既足遂不教而聽其自化也不
然何昔者陳王道於宣王乃於養民之後而必
曰謹庠序之教申之以孝弟之義觀此可以知
孟子發言之微意矣噫
===
易
外比於賢以從上也
方策
同考試官訓導鄭 批 此題場中士子易於
下筆而難於整齊其講比賢從上不覺失之
重複獨此卷提掇明白略無贅辭必精於說
易者高薦何忝
考試官教諭姜 批 聖人象傳之意正如
此子獨能闡明之殆熟於本領故也
punctuated:
可偏廢也？古帝王所以仁民之道，率不外此。然論其施為之序，則養民尤其急務。况戰國之時，民窮財盡，救死不贍，奚暇治禮義哉？故孟子於此章之論，獨歸重於養民之政。是雖有所感而發，亦曰教由養立，欲君人者先急其本，而後驅之善，非謂民食既足，遂不教而聽其自化也。不然，何昔者陳王道於宣王，乃於養民之後，而必曰：「謹庠序之教，申之以孝弟之義。」觀此，可以知孟子發言之微意矣。噫！
易
外比於賢，以從上也。
方策
同考試官訓導鄭批：此題場中士子易於下筆，而難於整齊。其講比賢從上，不覺失之重複。獨此卷提掇明白，略無贅辭，必精於說易者。高薦何忝？
考試官教諭姜批：聖人象傳之意，正如此。子獨能闡明之，殆熟於本領故也。
translation_en:
…could either be neglected? The means by which the ancient emperors and kings treated the people humanely generally extended no further than these. Yet, in considering the order of their implementation, providing for the people is especially urgent. Moreover, in the Warring States period, the people were impoverished and their resources exhausted; they could scarcely save themselves from death. What leisure had they to attend to ritual propriety and righteousness? Thus, in his discussion in this chapter, Mengzi places particular emphasis on policies that provide for the people. Although these words were prompted by particular circumstances, his point is also that teaching rests upon material provision. He wished rulers first to attend urgently to this foundation and afterward to guide the people toward goodness. He did not mean that, once the people had sufficient food, rulers should dispense with teaching and leave them to transform themselves. Otherwise, why, when he formerly expounded the kingly way to King Xuan, did he insist, after discussing provision for the people, on saying: “Attend carefully to instruction in the schools, reinforcing it with the duties of filial piety and respect for elder brothers”? From this we may understand the subtle intention behind Mengzi’s words. Ah!

Book of Changes

“He associates outwardly with the worthy, thereby following his superior.”

Fang Ce

Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Assistant Instructor: On this topic, candidates in the examination hall find it easy to begin writing but difficult to achieve an orderly composition. In explaining association with the worthy and following one’s superior, they unwittingly lapse into repetition. This paper alone brings out the essential points clearly, without a single superfluous phrase. Its author must be skilled in expounding the Book of Changes. How could recommending him for a high place be undeserved?

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Instructor: The sage’s meaning in the Commentary on the Images is precisely this. You alone have been able to elucidate it, presumably because you have thoroughly mastered the fundamentals.

title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
考試官敎諭張批說理明净
象傳論柔爻之進輔於有德以委身於明君也
夫德位兼隆之君臣子難逢之會也四得是君
而外輔之庸有不正而吉也哉昔周公於比之
六四既繫以外比之貞吉之辭矣吾夫子小象
從而申之謂夫比以得賢為貞臣願得君而事
彼六四也以柔正之德當親比之時位居承弼
固已出而比人矣而比得所比以有德者而為
依歸匪人之傷寧復有之身進廟堂固已出而
===
有輔矣而輔得所輔有賢人焉而為倚託失身
之誚誰能加之夫六四之外比於賢如此豈非
以其從上也哉誠以卦之九五剛健而純德邁
等倫矣而崇高是履巍然建極之大君普天之
下尊无二上者焉中正而粹賢超儔類矣而曆
數在躬赫然顯比之令主四海之廣仰惟一人
者焉四之外比正惟其以柔順之德而上輔於
此君光依日月之下所謂夙夜匪懈以事一人
者是已賛化調元何一而不可行者乎正惟其
punctuated:
考試官敎諭張批：說理明净。

象傳論柔爻之進輔於有德，以委身於明君也。夫德位兼隆之君，臣子難逢之會也。四得是君而外輔之，庸有不正而吉也哉？昔周公於比之六四，既繫以外比之貞吉之辭矣。吾夫子小象從而申之，謂夫比以得賢為貞，臣願得君而事。彼六四也，以柔正之德，當親比之時，位居承弼，固已出而比人矣。而比得所比，以有德者而為依歸，匪人之傷，寧復有之？身進廟堂，固已出而有輔矣。而輔得所輔，有賢人焉而為倚託，失身之誚，誰能加之？夫六四之外比於賢如此，豈非以其從上也哉？誠以卦之九五，剛健而純德，邁等倫矣。而崇高是履，巍然建極之大君，普天之下，尊无二上者焉。中正而粹賢，超儔類矣。而曆數在躬，赫然顯比之令主，四海之廣，仰惟一人者焉。四之外比，正惟其以柔順之德而上輔於此君，光依日月之下，所謂夙夜匪懈以事一人者是已。賛化調元，何一而不可行者乎？正惟其
translation_en:
Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: “The exposition of principle is clear and lucid.”

The Commentary on the Images discusses how the yielding line advances to assist one possessed of virtue, committing itself to an enlightened ruler. A ruler eminent in both virtue and position presents an opportunity that a minister seldom encounters. When the fourth line finds such a ruler and assists him by joining outwardly, how could this fail to be correct and auspicious?

Formerly, the Duke of Zhou appended to the fourth, yin line of Bi (Holding Together) the words concerning the constancy and good fortune of joining outwardly. Our Master Confucius then elaborated on them in the Lesser Commentary on the Images. His meaning is that, in joining with another, finding a worthy person constitutes constancy: a minister desires to find a ruler whom he can serve. That fourth, yin line, with its yielding and correct virtue, encounters a time of close association and occupies a position of support and assistance. It has indeed already come forth to join with another. Moreover, it joins with one whom it ought to join, taking a virtuous person as its refuge. How could it again suffer the harm of associating with an unworthy person? Having advanced into the court, it has indeed come forth to offer assistance. Moreover, it assists one whom it ought to assist, having a worthy person upon whom to rely. Who could reproach it for committing itself to the wrong person?

That the fourth, yin line thus joins outwardly with the worthy—is this not because it follows the one above? Indeed, the fifth, yang line of the hexagram is strong and vigorous, with pure virtue surpassing its peers. It occupies the loftiest position: a towering sovereign who establishes the supreme standard, whose supremacy admits no second throughout all under Heaven. Central and correct, of unalloyed worthiness, it surpasses all its fellows. The succession ordained by Heaven rests in its person: a splendid and excellent ruler who manifests the way of holding together, the one person to whom all within the vast Four Seas look up.

The fourth line’s outward joining occurs precisely because, with yielding and compliant virtue, it assists this ruler above, basking beneath the radiance of the sun and moon. This is what is meant by “Serving the One Man tirelessly, morning and night.” Assisting the transforming work of Heaven and Earth and harmonizing the primal forces—what among these could it not carry out? It is precisely because it…

title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
以柔正之臣而順麗乎大明誠同葵藿之傾所
謂忠順不失以事其上者是已立德立功有一
之不得遂者乎是則五之為君間世而一出四
之從五千載而一時得正而吉也顧不宜哉大
抵君臣之分雖相懸君臣之道未始不相須也
故君不得臣則无以行其萬化臣不得君亦无
以展其平生但自古昔以來有其君者未必有
其臣有其臣者未必遇其君相須之殷相值之
難唐虞賡歌所以曠千古而一見也然則四之
===
於五何幸而躬逢夫子於四寧不喜談而樂道
之也哉噫唐虞遠矣求其上下交而成德業者
深有望於
今日
是以明於天之道而察於民之故是興神
物以前民用
李高
同考試官訓導鄭 批 說出聖人作易之由
與教人之意詳盡可錄可錄
punctuated:
以柔正之臣而順麗乎大明，誠同葵藿之傾，所謂「忠順不失，以事其上」者是已。立德立功，有一之不得遂者乎？是則五之為君，間世而一出；四之從五，千載而一時。得正而吉也，顧不宜哉？大抵君臣之分雖相懸，君臣之道未始不相須也。故君不得臣，則无以行其萬化；臣不得君，亦无以展其平生。但自古昔以來，有其君者未必有其臣，有其臣者未必遇其君。相須之殷，相值之難，唐虞賡歌所以曠千古而一見也。然則四之於五，何幸而躬逢！夫子於四，寧不喜談而樂道之也哉？噫！唐虞遠矣，求其上下交而成德業者，深有望於今日。

是以明於天之道，而察於民之故，是興神物以前民用。

李高

同考試官訓導鄭批：說出聖人作《易》之由與教人之意，詳盡可錄，可錄。
translation_en:
…as a yielding yet upright minister, he obediently attaches himself to the great brightness of his sovereign. His sincerity resembles the sunflower and bean leaves turning toward the sun. This is what is meant by “serving one’s superior without failing in loyalty and obedience.” In establishing virtue and achieving merit, could there be anything he cannot accomplish? Thus, a ruler such as the fifth line represents appears only once in many generations; the fourth line’s opportunity to follow the fifth comes but once in a thousand years. Having attained correctness, it enjoys good fortune: is this not fitting?

Generally speaking, although ruler and minister stand far apart in rank, their respective ways have always depended upon one another. Without a minister, the ruler has no means of carrying out his myriad transforming influences; without a ruler, the minister likewise has no means of realizing his lifelong aspirations. Yet from ancient times onward, the presence of such a ruler has not necessarily meant the presence of such a minister, and such a minister has not necessarily encountered such a ruler. So profound is their mutual dependence, and so difficult their meeting, that the responsive songs of ruler and ministers in the age of Tang and Yu stand as a unique occurrence across the ages. How fortunate, then, that the fourth line should personally encounter the fifth! How could the Master fail to speak of the fourth with joy and delight? Alas! The age of Tang and Yu is far distant. For superiors and subordinates to unite and thereby accomplish works of virtue and merit, we place profound hopes in the present day.

“Therefore, understanding the Way of Heaven and discerning the circumstances of the people, they brought forth the sacred objects to guide the people in their use.”

Li Gao

Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Assistant Instructor: “The essay explains why the sages made the Book of Changes and their intention in teaching people. Thorough and comprehensive; worthy of inclusion, worthy of inclusion.”

title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
考試官教諭姜批題本冠冕而文亦官
樣錄之
考試官教諭張批切實簡當
聖人通天人之理有以肇卜筮之用焉夫一貫
天人聖心之妙契也如是而作為卜筮以教人
易之用豈不大行於天下哉大傳此章專論卜
筮及此謂夫易理既體具於聖心易教必興行
於天下是故天道幽遠而難明者也聖人纖塵
不染有以洞燭其潜庸默運之機若何而變化
===
若何而生成難明者於是乎大明矣民故浩繁
而難察者也聖人內境常清有以周知夫民生
日用之故如何而得失如何而憂虞難察者於
是乎畢察矣夫天道明則知蓍龜靈氣之所鍾
而可與其用民故察則知生民趨避之莫識而
當開其先於是興蓍以筮用之四十有九分揲
掛扐之法以立興龜以卜鑽之七十有二雨霽
蒙驛克之兆以見用靜用作作者賴以指迷豊功
於是乎肇啓矣有為有行者資其賛決大業于
punctuated:
考試官教諭姜批：題本冠冕，而文亦官樣，錄之。
考試官教諭張批：切實簡當。
聖人通天人之理，有以肇卜筮之用焉。夫一貫天人，聖心之妙契也。如是而作為卜筮以教人，易之用豈不大行於天下哉？大傳此章專論卜筮，及此謂夫易理既體具於聖心，易教必興行於天下。是故天道幽遠而難明者也，聖人纖塵不染，有以洞燭其潜庸默運之機，若何而變化，若何而生成，難明者於是乎大明矣。民故浩繁而難察者也，聖人內境常清，有以周知夫民生日用之故，如何而得失，如何而憂虞，難察者於是乎畢察矣。夫天道明，則知蓍龜靈氣之所鍾，而可與其用；民故察，則知生民趨避之莫識，而當開其先。於是興蓍以筮，用之四十有九，分揲掛扐之法以立；興龜以卜，鑽之七十有二，雨霽蒙驛克之兆以見。用靜用作作者，賴以指迷，豊功於是乎肇啓矣；有為有行者，資其賛決，大業于
translation_en:
Examiner Jiang, Instructor, comments: “The topic itself is dignified, and the composition likewise conforms to the official style. Include it.”
Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: “Substantial, concise, and apt.”
The sage comprehends the principles of Heaven and humanity and thereby initiates the use of divination with tortoise shells and milfoil stalks. A single thread uniting Heaven and humanity is the wondrous accord achieved by the sage’s mind. When, on this basis, he establishes divination to instruct people, how could the use of the Changes fail to spread widely throughout the world? This chapter of the Great Commentary discusses divination exclusively. At this point it means that, since the principles of the Changes are fully embodied in the sage’s mind, its teachings must be brought into practice throughout the world.
Thus, the Way of Heaven is hidden and remote, difficult to comprehend. Untainted by even the slightest dust, the sage can illuminate its hidden, silently operating workings [?]: how they bring about transformation and how they generate and complete things. What was difficult to comprehend thereby becomes abundantly clear. Human affairs are vast and numerous, difficult to discern. With his inner realm always clear, the sage can comprehend fully the circumstances of people’s daily lives: how gain and loss arise, and how worry and anxiety arise. What was difficult to discern is thereby discerned in full.
When the Way of Heaven is understood, he knows that milfoil and tortoises are where numinous energy gathers, and that their efficacy may be drawn upon. When human affairs are discerned, he knows that people do not understand what to pursue and what to avoid, and that he should provide them with guidance in advance. He therefore introduces milfoil for stalk divination, using forty-nine stalks, and establishes the methods of dividing, counting, setting aside, and retaining the remainders. He introduces tortoise shells for shell divination, drilling seventy-two hollows, so that the signs called rain, clearing, clouding, crossing, and overcoming become manifest. Those resting or undertaking activity [?] rely on these to find their way out of confusion; great achievements thus begin to unfold. Those embarking on undertakings and taking action draw upon their aid in reaching decisions; great enterprises, at …

title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
此乎開先矣是則聖人之通天人而立卜筮如
此則利生民澤後世厥功何如其大哉大抵有
人心之易有造化之易有易書之易神知易貢
之德易之具於聖心者也天道民故之類易之
見於造化者也至於畫卦卜筮易始載於易書
矣非聖心有易无以通乎造化非造化有易无
以會乎聖心非筆之於書則易將自造化聖人
而止耳百姓何以與其能哉此三才合一之道
也學者求易於易不若求於造化求於造化不
===
若求於吾心
書
德日新萬邦惟懷
吳顯宗
同考試官教諭鄭 批 德日新一句是古人
心離合之機至下文懋德建中方是作工夫處
士子多以仲虺勉成湯如此用工殊戾本旨是
篇依傳註敷衍明白而辭理蔚然其必深
於書者歟
punctuated:
此乎開先矣。是則聖人之通天人而立卜筮如此，則利生民、澤後世，厥功何如其大哉！大抵有人心之易，有造化之易，有易書之易。神知易貢之德，易之具於聖心者也；天道民故之類，易之見於造化者也；至於畫卦卜筮，易始載於易書矣。非聖心有易，无以通乎造化；非造化有易，无以會乎聖心；非筆之於書，則易將自造化聖人而止耳，百姓何以與其能哉？此三才合一之道也。學者求易於易，不若求於造化；求於造化，不若求於吾心。
書
德日新，萬邦惟懷。
吳顯宗
同考試官教諭鄭批：「德日新一句，是古人心離合之機。至下文懋德建中，方是作工夫處。士子多以仲虺勉成湯如此用工，殊戾本旨。是篇依傳註敷衍明白，而辭理蔚然，其必深於書者歟？」
translation_en:
…here the way is opened in advance. Such was the sages’ establishment of divination by tortoise shells and milfoil through their understanding of Heaven and humanity. How great, then, was their achievement in benefiting the people and extending blessings to later generations! Broadly speaking, there are the Changes within the human mind, the Changes within the workings of creation, and the Changes within the Book of Changes. The virtues of numinous understanding and of ease and tribute [?] are the Changes inherent in the sages’ minds. Such things as the Way of Heaven and human affairs are the Changes manifested in creation. Only with the drawing of hexagrams and divination by tortoise shells and milfoil did the Changes begin to be recorded in the Book of Changes. Without the Changes in the sages’ minds, there would be no means of comprehending creation; without the Changes in creation, there would be no means of corresponding with the sages’ minds. Without committing them to writing, the Changes would have remained confined to creation and the sages. How could the common people have shared in their efficacy? This is the Way by which the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity—are united as one. For students, seeking the Changes in the Book of Changes is less effective than seeking them in creation; seeking them in creation is less effective than seeking them in one’s own mind.
Book of Documents
“When virtue is renewed daily, the myriad states cherish their ruler.”
Wu Xianzong
Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor: “The phrase ‘virtue is renewed daily’ concerns the pivotal point at which the hearts of the ancients [?] turn away or come together. Only in the subsequent words, ‘make virtue abundant and establish the mean,’ do we reach the actual work of cultivation. Examination candidates commonly take this to mean that Zhonghui was urging Cheng Tang to apply himself in this way, which seriously contradicts the original intent. This essay develops its explanation clearly in accordance with the commentary and annotations, and its language and reasoning are richly accomplished. Surely its author has a profound understanding of the Book of Documents?”

title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
考試官教諭姜批新德萬邦懷處發揮
明白
考試官教諭張批人君新德而懷諸侯
此作深合傳意
一人之脩德無間其功羣辟之仰德無間其地
盖德乃繫屬天下之本也人君脩德而能常其
功則諸侯之仰德寧有間乎仲虺勸勉成湯統
御諸侯之道有如此其意若謂君天下以德為
本君德之脩否係萬邦之向背王可不益脩其
===
德而思所以繫其心乎是故奮剛健不息之誠
顧天明命而疏瀹之功視昔為有加雖日孜孜
也持謙冲不滿之心懷帝降衷而澡雪之力視
昔為彌篤終日乾乾也敬以直內存養于念慮
之微大政如是微言如是渣滓消融而萬象為
之森羅湛然全體之無瑕義以方外省察於事
為之著大廷如是深宮如是邪穢蕩滌而萬幾
為之俱新昭然大用之不昧如是則一德有恒
足以收人心之放一德無貳足以合天下之離
punctuated:
考試官教諭姜批：「新德萬邦懷處，發揮明白。」
考試官教諭張批：「人君新德而懷諸侯，此作深合傳意。」
一人之脩德，無間其功；羣辟之仰德，無間其地。盖德乃繫屬天下之本也。人君脩德而能常其功，則諸侯之仰德寧有間乎？仲虺勸勉成湯統御諸侯之道，有如此。其意若謂：君天下以德為本，君德之脩否，係萬邦之向背，王可不益脩其德，而思所以繫其心乎？是故奮剛健不息之誠，顧天明命，而疏瀹之功視昔為有加，雖日孜孜也；持謙冲不滿之心，懷帝降衷，而澡雪之力視昔為彌篤，終日乾乾也。敬以直內，存養于念慮之微，大政如是，微言如是，渣滓消融，而萬象為之森羅，湛然全體之無瑕；義以方外，省察於事為之著，大廷如是，深宮如是，邪穢蕩滌，而萬幾為之俱新，昭然大用之不昧。如是，則一德有恒，足以收人心之放；一德無貳，足以合天下之離。
translation_en:
Examiner Jiang, Instructor, comments: “The passage on renewing virtue and winning the allegiance of the myriad states develops its meaning clearly.”
Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: “The ruler renews his virtue and thereby wins the allegiance of the feudal lords. This composition accords deeply with the commentary’s meaning.”
The sovereign’s cultivation of virtue admits no interruption in effort; the many lords’ admiration for that virtue admits no distinction of place. For virtue is the foundation that binds all under Heaven together. If the ruler cultivates virtue with unwavering effort, how could the feudal lords’ admiration for it admit any interruption? Such was Zhonghui’s exhortation to Cheng Tang concerning the way to govern the feudal lords. His meaning was as though to say: “Ruling all under Heaven rests upon virtue. Whether the ruler cultivates his virtue determines whether the myriad states turn toward him or away from him. Can the king fail to cultivate his virtue still further and consider how to bind their hearts to him?”
Thus he rouses a sincerity that is vigorous and unceasing, keeps Heaven’s luminous mandate in view, and increases his efforts to clear and cleanse his mind beyond what they were before, diligently applying himself each day [?]. He maintains a humble heart free from complacency, cherishes the moral nature bestowed by the Lord on High, and makes his efforts at purification still more earnest than before, exerting himself tirelessly throughout the day. Through reverent attentiveness he makes his inner self upright, preserving and nurturing it amid the subtlest stirrings of thought: so it is in great affairs of government, and so it is in the slightest utterance. Impurities dissolve, and the myriad forms stand arrayed in their fullness; his entire being is limpid and without blemish. Through righteousness he makes his outward conduct square, examining himself in manifest deeds and affairs: so it is in the great court, and so it is in the inner palace. Evil and defilement are swept away, and the myriad affairs of government are all renewed; the full operation of his virtue is luminous and unobscured. In this way, constancy in his single virtue suffices to gather back the people’s straying hearts, and undivided commitment to that virtue suffices to reunite all that is divided under Heaven…

title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
萬邦雖遠焉有不懷者乎振舉於此而遠者聞
焉思欲望闕廷而納欵鼓舞于風聲之下蓋異
地而同心軌範於此而遠者效焉思欲依衮冕
而稽顙沐浴於德教之中蓋殊方而一志曰朝
曰覲顒然六服承德之休殆若萬派之必趨乎
東也曰會曰同翕然庶邦丕享之盛殆若眾星
之必拱乎北也夫有天下而為天下君必君德
新而萬邦懷則人心之收放合離其本固有在
而其機亦可畏也王可不思所以盡今日之責
===
而徒為來世之恐哉抑仲虺是篇為釋成湯之
慚而作也愚嘗因是竊疑前古聖人順天應人
心事光明顧尤恐恐然有不勝之情不滿之懷
而其輔弼大臣開釋勸諭無慮數百言要之不
過述天命本人情諄諄乎脩德檢身之說終不
敢指其心事之底蘊直謂其必無以破其跼蹐
不寧之心則其在上不似失之迂而在下不似
失之泛乎夫君臣之際關天下古今之大防此
正見有商君臣心之不容已言之不苟發出
punctuated:
萬邦雖遠，焉有不懷者乎？振舉於此，而遠者聞焉，思欲望闕廷而納欵，鼓舞于風聲之下，蓋異地而同心。軌範於此，而遠者效焉，思欲依衮冕而稽顙，沐浴於德教之中，蓋殊方而一志。曰朝曰覲，顒然六服承德之休，殆若萬派之必趨乎東也；曰會曰同，翕然庶邦丕享之盛，殆若眾星之必拱乎北也。夫有天下而為天下君，必君德新而萬邦懷，則人心之收放合離，其本固有在，而其機亦可畏也。王可不思所以盡今日之責，而徒為來世之恐哉？
抑仲虺是篇，為釋成湯之慚而作也。愚嘗因是竊疑：前古聖人，順天應人，心事光明，顧尤恐恐然，有不勝之情、不滿之懷；而其輔弼大臣，開釋勸諭，無慮數百言，要之不過述天命、本人情，諄諄乎脩德檢身之說，終不敢指其心事之底蘊，直謂其必無，以破其跼蹐不寧之心。則其在上，不似失之迂，而在下，不似失之泛乎？夫君臣之際，關天下古今之大防，此正見有商君臣心之不容已、言之不苟發，出
translation_en:
Though the myriad states lie far away, how could any fail to turn to him in allegiance? When worthy conduct is upheld here, those far away hear of it and long to face the palace court and offer their allegiance. Inspired by the reports of his influence, they share one heart despite dwelling in different lands. When exemplary standards are established here, those far away emulate them and long to draw near the ruler in his ceremonial robes and crown and bow their foreheads to the ground. Bathed in his virtuous instruction, they share one purpose despite coming from different regions. At the spring and autumn audiences, the six zones of allegiance reverently receive the blessings of his virtue, much as countless streams inevitably flow eastward. At assemblies and general gatherings, the many states unite in the magnificent presentation of their offerings, much as the stars inevitably cluster about the northern pole. For one who possesses All-under-Heaven and rules as its sovereign, it is essential that his virtue be renewed and the myriad states turn to him in allegiance. Thus, whether people’s hearts are gathered in or scattered, united or divided, assuredly has its root; and the workings that determine this are indeed to be held in awe. Could the king fail to consider how to fulfill his responsibilities today, and merely fear the judgment of later ages?
Now, this piece by Zhong Hui was written to dispel Cheng Tang’s shame. Reflecting on this, I have ventured in my ignorance to wonder: the sage of antiquity followed Heaven and responded to the people; his intentions and deeds were clear and upright. Yet he remained deeply apprehensive, feeling unequal to his task and dissatisfied with himself. His great minister and counselor offered explanations, encouragement, and admonition in several hundred words. In essence, however, these merely expounded Heaven’s mandate, grounded themselves in human sentiments, and earnestly urged the cultivation of virtue and restraint of the self. He never dared point directly to the innermost truth of the king’s intentions and deeds and state outright that there was certainly no cause for shame, thereby dispelling his constrained and uneasy state of mind. Does this not make the ruler above seem excessively scrupulous, and the minister below excessively vague? Yet the relationship between ruler and minister concerns the great safeguards of All-under-Heaven, past and present. Here we see precisely how the ruler and minister of Shang could not suppress what was in their hearts and did not speak carelessly, going forth…

title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
於常情之外者先民謂此心之慚此誥之釋皆
不可無吁旨哉
自朝至于日中昃不遑暇食
朱鵬
同考試官教諭鄭批不遑暇食是言文王
勤政之心雖一食之頃有不遑暇非言文王果於
不食也作者多昧此意此篇說出文王不暇逸之
心明白痛快非有心得者不能到此宜取之以冠
本房
===
考試官教諭姜批文王勤勞之心此作
可想見
考試官教諭張批發出文王無逸之心
時已周於一日心不逸於終食聖王勤政事然
也甚矣聖王圖治之切也一日之周而無終食
之逸其勤於政事也如此哉昔周公舉文王之
無逸以告成王此則言其勤政事意謂有國家
者未有不以勤而興盍不觀我周之文王乎自
朝至于日之中計一日之晷時之更涉悠悠乎
punctuated:
於常情之外者。先民謂此心之慚、此誥之釋，皆不可無。吁，旨哉！

「自朝至于日中昃，不遑暇食。」
朱鵬

同考試官教諭鄭批：不遑暇食，是言文王勤政之心，雖一食之頃，有不遑暇，非言文王果於不食也。作者多昧此意，此篇說出文王不暇逸之心，明白痛快，非有心得者不能到此。宜取之以冠本房。

考試官教諭姜批：文王勤勞之心，此作可想見。

考試官教諭張批：發出文王無逸之心。

時已周於一日，心不逸於終食，聖王勤政事然也。甚矣，聖王圖治之切也！一日之周，而無終食之逸，其勤於政事也如此哉！昔周公舉文王之無逸以告成王，此則言其勤政事。意謂有國家者，未有不以勤而興，盍不觀我周之文王乎？自朝至于日之中，計一日之晷，時之更涉，悠悠乎
translation_en:
…beyond ordinary human feelings. Earlier worthies said that neither this shame in his heart nor the reassurance offered by this announcement could be dispensed with. Ah, how profound!

“From morning until midday and the sun’s decline, he had no leisure to eat.”
By Zhu Peng.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor: “He had no leisure to eat” describes King Wen’s devotion to government: even for the time it takes to eat a meal, he felt he had no leisure. It does not mean that King Wen actually went without eating. Writers often miss this meaning. This essay conveys King Wen’s unwillingness to take his ease with clarity and force. Without personal insight, its author could not have reached this level. It should be selected to head the essays from this examining room.

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Instructor: King Wen’s diligent spirit can be imagined from this composition.

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Instructor: It brings out King Wen’s resolve to shun ease.

Time runs through an entire day, yet his heart takes no rest even for the duration of a meal: such is the sage king’s diligence in affairs of government. How earnest is the sage king’s pursuit of good governance! Throughout the whole day, he enjoys no respite even for a meal. Such is his diligence in governing!

Long ago, the Duke of Zhou cited King Wen’s avoidance of ease to admonish King Cheng. Here he speaks of King Wen’s diligence in government. His meaning is that those who rule a state have never flourished except through diligence. Why, then, should we not look to King Wen of our Zhou? From morning until midday, reckoning the day’s passage by the sundial, the hours pass on and on…

title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
巳居一日之半歷時固不淺也自中至于日之
昃計一日之運時之更閱綿綿乎已盡一日之
終歷時固何多也人之大情自謂享有天下孰
不欲珍饈迭舉於移時醉飽為歡於終日文王
之心則以為一政未脩畎畝之艱難係焉一事
未舉閭巷之怨詛關焉求治如渴而憂勤之心
恒存於旦晝之頃視民如傷而惕勵之念每切
於朝夕之間或朝而饔歟為時特轉移也一朝
饔之不遑文王非要譽也精神所運惟欲納庶
===
政於惟和之域汲汲乎規畫之周詳心自有不
遑耳或暮而飧歟為時特奄忽也一暮飧之不
暇文王非矯情也意念所注惟欲措庶事於惟
康之境皇皇乎綜理之微密心自有不暇耳即
一日而一歲一月之日可因而類推舉一食而
一身一家之奉可由而例見文王之勤政事如
此今王為文王之文孫而嗣有文王之大業烏
可不思所以法文王以慰其在天之靈哉抑周
公斯言特文王無逸中之一節耳然要之君人
punctuated: 巳居一日之半，歷時固不淺也。自中至于日之昃，計一日之運，時之更閱，綿綿乎已盡一日之終，歷時固何多也！人之大情，自謂享有天下，孰不欲珍饈迭舉於移時，醉飽為歡於終日？文王之心則以為：一政未脩，畎畝之艱難係焉；一事未舉，閭巷之怨詛關焉。求治如渴，而憂勤之心恒存於旦晝之頃；視民如傷，而惕勵之念每切於朝夕之間。或朝而饔歟？為時特轉移也。一朝饔之不遑，文王非要譽也。精神所運，惟欲納庶政於惟和之域，汲汲乎規畫之周詳，心自有不遑耳。或暮而飧歟？為時特奄忽也。一暮飧之不暇，文王非矯情也。意念所注，惟欲措庶事於惟康之境，皇皇乎綜理之微密，心自有不暇耳。即一日而一歲一月之日，可因而類推；舉一食而一身一家之奉，可由而例見。文王之勤政事如此。今王為文王之文孫，而嗣有文王之大業，烏可不思所以法文王，以慰其在天之靈哉？抑周公斯言，特文王無逸中之一節耳。然要之，君人
translation_en:
…half the day has already passed: the time elapsed is certainly not short. From noon until the sun declines, reckoning the course of a day, the hours pass on and on until the whole day is spent. How much time has elapsed! Such is ordinary human feeling that, considering oneself the possessor of all under Heaven, who would not wish to have delicacies served in succession for hours, taking pleasure all day in drinking and eating one's fill? Yet King Wen thought: if a single measure of government remains unattended to, the hardships of those in the fields depend upon it; if a single undertaking remains unperformed, the resentments and curses of those in the lanes are bound up with it. He thirsted for good government, and anxious diligence remained constantly in his heart throughout the day. He cared for the people as though they were injured, and thoughts of vigilance and exertion pressed upon him morning and evening.

Was it perhaps morning, time for the morning meal? The moment would pass in an instant. If he could not spare time for even one morning meal, King Wen was not seeking praise. He directed his energies solely toward bringing all affairs of government into harmony. Intent on making his plans thorough and comprehensive, he naturally felt he had no time to spare. Was it perhaps evening, time for the evening meal? The moment would slip away all too quickly. If he had no leisure for even one evening meal, King Wen was not feigning his feelings. His thoughts were fixed solely on bringing every undertaking to a state of well-being. Anxiously attending to the finest details of their coordination and management, he naturally felt he had no leisure.

From this single day, one may infer by analogy the days of a month or a year; from this one meal, one may likewise discern how he treated the provisions for his person and household. Such was King Wen's diligence in government. Now you, O King, are King Wen's illustrious grandson and have inherited his great enterprise. How could you fail to consider how to emulate King Wen and thereby comfort his spirit in Heaven? Yet these words of the Duke of Zhou concern only one aspect of King Wen's freedom from idleness. Nevertheless, in sum, for one who rules over others…

title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
著之大法亦孰有要于此者乎向使時君世主
深體而力行之必不至窮口腹之欲流連光景
萬事之所由必理萬民之所由必治召太和迎
善氣壽國脉而享長年盖有必然者噫有周八
百年有道之長孰謂不自文王一食之頃有不
遑暇中來哉
詩
文王受命有此武功既伐于崇作邑于豐
文王烝哉
===
王珵

title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
真作手也
聖人奉天伐暴而即有事於遷都此可見其克
君也盖伐暴畢而遷都繼舉所以為安民計也
聖人以之其克君也何如哉此詩言文王遷豐
之事意謂維我文王一德之敬止布而為遹求
厥寧之心上帝於是乎聿懷一德之小心運而
為遹觀厥成之念皇天於是乎默眷啓之詢仇
也則得專征伐昭然大命之有歸啓之去暴也
則載授鈇鉞居然成命之誕膺天命既受天討
===
斯行聲罪於倡亂之崇加兵於肆釁之國是伐
是肆鋤強梗於三旬之餘武功丕著於當時是
絕是忽除讒邪於一掃之後罪人斯得於授首
崇侯既伐則民歸日衆舊邑不能以盡容人心
咸歸則國勢浸盛新都不容於不作于焉相厥
山川而作邑于豐城池廟寢殆將煥剙慶於一
新干焉審其向背而建都于豐朝市祖社殆將
鼎規模於肇造舉國生靈盡携而東下民於此
乎王勃勃乎興王之氣象矣五廟鍾虡悉卷而
punctuated:
真作手也。

聖人奉天伐暴，而即有事於遷都，此可見其克君也。盖伐暴畢而遷都繼舉，所以為安民計也。聖人以之，其克君也何如哉？此詩言文王遷豐之事，意謂維我文王，一德之敬止，布而為遹求厥寧之心，上帝於是乎聿懷；一德之小心，運而為遹觀厥成之念，皇天於是乎默眷。啓之詢仇也，則得專征伐，昭然大命之有歸；啓之去暴也，則載授鈇鉞，居然成命之誕膺。天命既受，天討斯行。聲罪於倡亂之崇，加兵於肆釁之國，是伐是肆，鋤強梗於三旬之餘，武功丕著於當時；是絕是忽，除讒邪於一掃之後，罪人斯得於授首。崇侯既伐，則民歸日衆，舊邑不能以盡容；人心咸歸，則國勢浸盛，新都不容於不作。于焉相厥山川，而作邑于豐，城池廟寢，殆將煥剙慶於一新；干焉審其向背，而建都于豐，朝市祖社，殆將鼎規模於肇造。舉國生靈，盡携而東，下民於此乎王，勃勃乎興王之氣象矣！五廟鍾虡，悉卷而
translation_en:
…a true master of composition!

The sage obeyed Heaven in attacking the violent ruler and immediately undertook to move his capital. This shows his capacity to be a ruler. For once the campaign against violence was finished, the relocation of the capital followed: this was his plan for bringing peace to the people. The sage acted upon this principle—how great was his capacity to rule! This ode speaks of King Wen’s move to Feng. Its meaning is that our King Wen’s reverence, grounded in his single-minded virtue, extended into a resolve to seek peace for his people, and the Lord on High therefore cherished him. The watchfulness of that same virtue worked through his intention to observe the completion of his undertaking, and August Heaven therefore watched over him unseen. Heaven guided him to consult his allies, granting him sole authority to conduct punitive campaigns and clearly showing where the great Mandate had come to rest. Heaven guided him to remove violence, bestowing upon him the battle-axes of command, so that he manifestly received its settled Mandate in full. Having received Heaven’s Mandate, he carried out Heaven’s punishment.

He proclaimed the offenses of Chong, which had fomented disorder, and brought arms against the state that recklessly provoked conflict. He attacked and assaulted it, rooting out the stubbornly powerful after more than thirty days; his martial achievement shone forth in his own time. He cut off and destroyed them, sweeping away the slanderous and wicked at a single stroke; the guilty were brought to account when they surrendered their heads. Once the Marquis of Chong had been attacked, more people came over each day, and the old settlement could no longer accommodate them all. As the people’s hearts all turned to him, the strength of his state steadily increased, and a new capital had to be built.

Thereupon he surveyed the mountains and rivers and established a settlement at Feng. Its walls and moats, temples and residential halls would shine with the blessings of an entirely new foundation [?]. Thereupon [?] he examined its orientation and established his capital at Feng. Its court and markets, ancestral temples and altars of the soil would assume a grand design at their founding [?]. All the people of the realm were brought east together, and here he became king over the common people: how vigorously the signs of a rising royal house flourished! title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
行萬邦於此乎向駸駸乎一統之規模矣夫然
豈不為克君乎吾見崇侯伐而豐邑成非但拓
不拔之鴻基也而所以求厥寧者有其所文王
父母斯民信乎招徠之有道矣尚何有弗克耶
豐邑成而人心繫非但開無前之偉績也而所
以觀厥成者有其漸文王君臨億兆誠哉撫綏
之有方矣尚何有或斁耶旹方奉命以除暴而
即遷都以安民文王之克君如此詩人述而美
之宜矣大抵天以安民為心而文王乃安民之
主故伐崇雖所以奉天亦所以安民遷豐雖所
以安民亦所以奉天要皆有不容已者固非逞
私憤利土地之為也此所以重光乎先世繼述
之託大裕乎後世集統之事至武王而天下歸
周皇王維辟良有以哉後世若蠶食六國既非
本於奉天營朝宮渭南亦非本於安民其於君
道之得失較然矣噫周以八百秦以二世不為
無所自云
薄言震之莫不震疊懷柔百神及河喬嶽
punctuated:
行，萬邦於此乎向，駸駸乎一統之規模矣。夫然，豈不為克君乎？吾見崇侯伐而豐邑成，非但拓不拔之鴻基也，而所以求厥寧者有其所。文王父母斯民，信乎招徠之有道矣，尚何有弗克耶？豐邑成而人心繫，非但開無前之偉績也，而所以觀厥成者有其漸。文王君臨億兆，誠哉撫綏之有方矣，尚何有或斁耶？旹方奉命以除暴，而即遷都以安民，文王之克君如此，詩人述而美之宜矣。大抵天以安民為心，而文王乃安民之主，故伐崇雖所以奉天，亦所以安民；遷豐雖所以安民，亦所以奉天。要皆有不容已者，固非逞私憤、利土地之為也。此所以重光乎先世繼述之託，大裕乎後世集統之事。至武王而天下歸周，「皇王維辟」，良有以哉！後世若蠶食六國，既非本於奉天；營朝宮渭南，亦非本於安民。其於君道之得失，較然矣。噫！周以八百，秦以二世，不為無所自云。

薄言震之，莫不震疊。懷柔百神，及河喬嶽。
translation_en:
…went forth, and the myriad states turned toward him: swiftly the foundations of unified rule took shape. This being so, was he not truly capable of ruling? I see that, when the lord of Chong had been attacked and the city of Feng completed, this did more than establish a magnificent, unshakable foundation: it provided a place in which the people could seek repose. King Wen acted as father and mother to these people; truly, he knew how to attract them to him. How could there have been any failure in his rule? When Feng was completed and the people’s hearts were bound to him, this did more than inaugurate an unprecedented achievement: there was a gradual process through which its completion could be witnessed. King Wen ruled over the multitudes; truly, he knew how to comfort and settle them. How could there have been any disaffection? At that time, he had just obeyed Heaven’s command to eliminate tyranny when he moved his capital to bring peace to the people. Such was King Wen’s capacity to rule; fittingly, the poet recounted and praised it.

Heaven’s purpose, broadly speaking, is to bring peace to the people, and King Wen was a ruler who brought them peace. Thus, although attacking Chong served to obey Heaven, it also served to bring peace to the people; although moving to Feng served to bring peace to the people, it also served to obey Heaven. In each case, the action was something he could not forgo. Certainly he was not venting private resentment or seeking territorial gain. This is how he added fresh luster to the charge of carrying forward his forebears’ work and amply prepared the task of consolidating sovereign rule for later generations. By King Wu’s time, all under Heaven had submitted to Zhou. “The august king is sovereign”: indeed, there was good reason for this!

In later times, the piecemeal annexation of the six states was not grounded in obedience to Heaven; nor was the construction of the imperial palace south of the Wei River grounded in bringing peace to the people. Success and failure in the way of rulership are plainly distinguished here. Alas! That Zhou lasted eight hundred years and Qin only two generations was not without its causes.

He exerted his awe-inspiring power, and none failed to tremble and submit. He conciliated the hundred spirits, including those of the Yellow River and the lofty mountains.

When the king receives the assembled lords in audience, none fails to submit; when he sacrifices to the assembled spirits, none fails to come. Heaven’s favor toward the king of Zhou makes this so. For conducting inspection tours, receiving the lords in audience, and making sacrificial announcements are the foremost duties of one who possesses All under Heaven. Through a single undertaking, the king of Zhou sees both men and spirits assume their respective offices. Can one say that Heaven’s favor has no object? This is a ceremonial song for audiences and sacrificial announcements during an inspection tour. Its meaning is this: our king of Zhou has received High Heaven’s mandate to uphold the succession and performs the inspection rites of his dynasty. What, then, should be the evidence of their efficacy among men and spirits?

title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
邦家君仰王度之煥昭慮天威之莫測莫不稽
首稱藩而驚惕不遑在南霍者無異於東岱也
六服羣辟覩王綱之丕振知國憲之有常莫不
拱手聽命而戰懼不暇在北恒者無間於西華
也朝會之下寧有一人之不服者乎以祭告言
之鍾靈萃英於兩間百神非一類也今則置茅
蕝設表望凡其利澤及民而當祀者隨方致享
而懷安之不遺奠璧玉陳牲帛凡其功德在世
而當告者隨地克禋而招徠之有道以至深廣
===
莫如河至難格也一皆格之來格俯望秩而居
歆四瀆以之效靈不獨丘陵墳衍之屬然也崇
高莫如嶽至難享也一皆享之來享依燔柴而
昭鑒五嶽以之赫異不獨古昔聖賢之類然也
祭告之下寧有一神之不格者乎是則驗之明
而羣后服驗之幽而百神格人神受職天之右
序有周於斯見矣子我周王寧不為可必哉嗟
夫有天下而巡守人君所以親萬民之大綱馭
諸侯之大柄也以舜受堯禪尚不免朝羣后而
punctuated:
邦家君仰王度之煥昭，慮天威之莫測，莫不稽首稱藩而驚惕不遑。在南霍者，無異於東岱也。六服羣辟覩王綱之丕振，知國憲之有常，莫不拱手聽命而戰懼不暇。在北恒者，無間於西華也。朝會之下，寧有一人之不服者乎？以祭告言之，鍾靈萃英於兩間，百神非一類也。今則置茅蕝，設表望，凡其利澤及民而當祀者，隨方致享，而懷安之不遺；奠璧玉，陳牲帛，凡其功德在世而當告者，隨地克禋，而招徠之有道。以至深廣莫如河，至難格也，一皆格之。來格，俯望秩而居歆，四瀆以之效靈，不獨丘陵墳衍之屬然也。崇高莫如嶽，至難享也，一皆享之。來享，依燔柴而昭鑒，五嶽以之赫異，不獨古昔聖賢之類然也。祭告之下，寧有一神之不格者乎？是則驗之明而羣后服，驗之幽而百神格。人神受職，天之右序有周，於斯見矣。子我周王，寧不為可必哉？
嗟夫！有天下而巡守，人君所以親萬民之大綱、馭諸侯之大柄也。以舜受堯禪，尚不免朝羣后而
translation_en:
…the lords of the states looked up to the brilliance of the king’s ordinances and pondered the unfathomable majesty of Heaven. All bowed their heads to the ground and acknowledged themselves as his feudatories, anxious and awestruck without a moment’s ease. Those at southern Mount Huo were no different from those at eastern Mount Dai. The rulers of the six zones of submission beheld the great renewal of royal authority and understood that the laws of the realm were constant. All clasped their hands and obeyed his commands, trembling in fear without respite. Those at northern Mount Heng were no different from those at western Mount Hua. At these court assemblies, could there have been a single person who did not submit?
As for the sacrifices and announcements to the spirits, the hundred spirits, in whom the numinous forces and finest essences of Heaven and Earth gathered, were of many kinds. Now bundles of thatch were set out as ritual markers, and markers for distant sacrifices were erected. All whose benefits reached the people and who deserved sacrifice received offerings in their respective regions; none was neglected in being comforted and set at ease. Jade discs and other jades were laid out, and sacrificial animals and silk were presented. All whose achievements and virtue had benefited the world and who deserved ritual announcements received pure sacrifices in their respective places; there was a proper way to summon them and bring them near. In depth and breadth, nothing equaled the Yellow River, whose spirit was exceedingly difficult to induce to come; yet all were brought to attend. Coming, they looked down upon the distant sacrifices offered according to rank and remained to savor them. Through this, the Four Waterways manifested their spiritual power; it was not only the spirits of hills, mounds, riverbanks, and plains that did so. In lofty height, nothing equaled the sacred mountains, whose spirits were exceedingly difficult to induce to accept offerings; yet all were brought to partake. Coming to partake, they drew near the burning sacrificial wood and gazed down with luminous discernment. Through this, the Five Sacred Mountains manifested their wondrous power; it was not only the sages and worthies of antiquity who did so. At these sacrifices and ritual announcements, could there have been a single spirit who did not come?
Thus, tested in the visible realm, the many lords submitted; tested in the unseen realm, the hundred spirits came. Humans and spirits fulfilled their duties: Heaven’s favor toward and ordering of Zhou could be seen in this. Could it not be certain that Heaven cherished our king of Zhou as its son [?]?
Alas! For one who possesses all under Heaven, tours of inspection are the sovereign’s great means of drawing close to the myriad people and his great instrument for governing the regional lords. Even Shun, who received the throne through Yao’s abdication, still had to hold an audience with the many lords and…

造詞謹嚴能斷悼公之得失結尤有餘味佳士也
考試官教諭姜批使悼公復生亦當心服
考試官教諭張批文字得春秋謹嚴之法
霸主講信以要貳春秋著其非推誠以服貳春
秋著其美觀晉悼公之處鄭有以見盟不足恃
而誠足以感人也春秋始書盟而終書會得失
較然矣何則鄭在春秋實南北之樞紐為夷夏
之重輕中國得鄭則可以拒楚楚得鄭則可以
punctuated:
徧羣神，況武王革命之主乎？今觀其巡守，以諸侯則震驚，以羣神則感格，要皆非人力所能為也。此所以比殷頌之、于邁頌之，而為萬世之美談也歟？後世有東封泰山為足以誇耀列國，西幸汾陰為足以讋服四海，其於先王□□之意何如耶？愚於此深感武王之盡君道。
春秋
「同盟于亳城北」、「會于蕭魚」，俱襄公十一年。
翟務實
同考試官教諭杜批：是篇以盟誠立說，而造詞謹嚴，能斷悼公之得失，結尤有餘味，佳士也。
考試官教諭姜批：使悼公復生，亦當心服。
考試官教諭張批：文字得春秋謹嚴之法。
霸主講信以要貳，春秋著其非；推誠以服貳，春秋著其美。觀晉悼公之處鄭，有以見盟不足恃，而誠足以感人也。春秋始書盟，而終書會，得失較然矣。何則？鄭在春秋，實南北之樞紐，為夷夏之重輕。中國得鄭，則可以拒楚；楚得鄭，則可以
translation_en:
…and extend his rites to all the spirits, how much more was this incumbent upon King Wu, who had brought about a change of dynasty? Now, examining his inspection tours, we see that the feudal lords were awestruck and the spirits were moved to respond and come into his presence. In essence, none of this could have been achieved by human effort alone. Was this why he was celebrated in the hymns in comparison with Yin and for his royal progress [?], becoming a subject of admiration for all ages? In later times, some regarded traveling east to perform the Feng sacrifice on Mount Tai as sufficient to impress the assembled states, or journeying west to Fenyin as sufficient to overawe all within the Four Seas. How did these compare with the former kings’ intention of □□? Here I am deeply moved by how fully King Wu fulfilled the Way of the ruler.
Spring and Autumn Annals
“They jointly covenanted north of Bocheng”; “They met at Xiaoyu.” Both entries are from the eleventh year of Duke Xiang.
Di Wushi
Comment by Associate Examiner Du, Instructor: This essay builds its argument around covenants and sincerity. Its wording is careful and exact, and it successfully judges Duke Dao’s successes and failures. The conclusion is especially rich in lingering implications. A worthy scholar!
Comment by Examiner Jiang, Instructor: Were Duke Dao to return to life, even he would surely be convinced at heart.
Comment by Examiner Zhang, Instructor: The writing captures the careful precision of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
When a hegemon invokes good faith to bind those of divided allegiance, the Spring and Autumn Annals records his error; when he extends sincerity to win their submission, it records his merit. Examining Duke Dao of Jin’s handling of Zheng, we can see that covenants cannot be relied upon, whereas sincerity can move people. The Spring and Autumn Annals first records a covenant and finally records a meeting: success and failure stand clearly distinguished. Why is this? During the Spring and Autumn period, Zheng was truly the pivot between north and south; it determined the balance of power between the foreign peoples and the Chinese states. If the central states secured Zheng, they could resist Chu; if Chu secured Zheng, it could…

title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
拒中國犧牲玉帛待於境上固其常態也今也
悼公復覇爭鄭於楚鄭人乃於三駕之餘特為
行成之舉使悼公於此能早見預待而御之有
術吾知鄭雖反覆不常敢不自服乎胡乃惑於
范宣子之見又為亳城北之盟救災患恤禍亂
非不美也未免事盟詛之澆風獎王室同好惡
非不善也不能脫牲歃之薄俗是以壇坫未掃
口血尚腥而鄭又從楚伐宋雖渝隊命亡氏之
言踣其國家之語莫之顧也是何慢鬼神至於
===
此極耶良由悼公要之以盟爾要之以盟固不
能服鄭而楚染指垂涎之念其肯休乎是故春
秋特書曰同盟于亳城北者非志同欲也惡鄭
反覆而悼公不臧之謀自見矣既而諸侯伐鄭
東門觀兵鄭人又遣伯駢之使復為請會之舉
使悼公於此不改弦易轍而服之無道吾知鄭
雖從違有在其肯心服乎幸而聽夫魏絳之謀
不事盟誓之末禮鄭囚遣歸國而一誠相與無
猜忌之心納斥候禁侵掠而二氣相孚無疑問
punctuated: 拒中國。犧牲玉帛待於境上，固其常態也。今也悼公復覇，爭鄭於楚，鄭人乃於三駕之餘，特為行成之舉。使悼公於此能早見預待，而御之有術，吾知鄭雖反覆不常，敢不自服乎？胡乃惑於范宣子之見，又為亳城北之盟？救災患，恤禍亂，非不美也，未免事盟詛之澆風；獎王室，同好惡，非不善也，不能脫牲歃之薄俗。是以壇坫未掃，口血尚腥，而鄭又從楚伐宋。雖渝隊命亡氏之言、踣其國家之語，莫之顧也。是何慢鬼神至於此極耶？良由悼公要之以盟爾。要之以盟，固不能服鄭，而楚染指垂涎之念，其肯休乎？是故《春秋》特書曰「同盟于亳城北」者，非志同欲也，惡鄭反覆，而悼公不臧之謀自見矣。既而諸侯伐鄭，東門觀兵，鄭人又遣伯駢之使，復為請會之舉。使悼公於此不改弦易轍，而服之無道，吾知鄭雖從違有在，其肯心服乎？幸而聽夫魏絳之謀，不事盟誓之末禮。鄭囚遣歸國，而一誠相與，無猜忌之心；納斥候，禁侵掠，而二氣相孚，無疑問
translation_en:
…resist the Central States. Keeping sacrificial animals, jade, and silk ready at the border was indeed Zheng’s habitual practice. Now Duke Dao had restored his hegemony and was contending with Chu for Zheng. Only after three campaigns did the people of Zheng make a particular move to negotiate peace. Had Duke Dao at this point foreseen matters, prepared beforehand, and employed proper methods to manage Zheng, I know that, however fickle Zheng might have been, it would hardly have dared refuse submission. Why, then, was he misled by Fan Xuanzi’s views into making yet another covenant, north of Bocheng? Providing relief in disasters and succoring those afflicted by calamity and disorder were certainly admirable, yet these commitments still partook of the degenerate fashion for covenants and imprecations. Supporting the royal house and sharing common likes and dislikes were certainly good, yet they could not escape the debased custom of sacrificing animals and smearing the lips with blood. Thus, before the covenant altar and its furnishings had been cleared away, while the blood on their lips still smelled fresh, Zheng again followed Chu in attacking Song. Zheng paid no heed to the words threatening loss of life and extinction of the clan for a breach [?], or to the pronouncement that its state would be overthrown. How could disregard for the spirits have reached such an extreme? It was precisely because Duke Dao sought to bind Zheng by a covenant. Binding it by a covenant could not secure its submission; would Chu then willingly abandon its covetous desire to meddle and take a share?

Thus, when the Spring and Autumn Annals specifically records, “They made a joint covenant north of Bocheng,” it is not recording a common purpose. It condemns Zheng’s vacillation, while the unsoundness of Duke Dao’s strategy becomes apparent of itself. Subsequently, the lords attacked Zheng and displayed their troops at its eastern gate. The people of Zheng again sent Bo Pian as an envoy and once more requested a meeting. Had Duke Dao at this point failed to change course, possessing no proper means of securing submission, I know that, although Zheng had its reasons for obedience or defiance, it would hardly have submitted sincerely. Fortunately, he listened to Wei Jiang’s counsel and did not concern himself with the superficial formalities of covenants and oaths. Zheng’s captives were sent back to their state, and he dealt with Zheng in wholehearted sincerity, harboring no suspicion or jealousy. He recalled the scouts and prohibited incursions and plundering, so that the two sides trusted one another in spirit, without doubt…

title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
之念由是兵車百乘歌鍾二肆而鄭之賂晉益
厚雖被良霄之執二十四年之久莫敢叛也是
何遵約束至於許遠耶良由悼公感之以誠爾
感之以誠固足以服鄭而楚人狼貪虎噬之毒
自不敢肆矣是故春秋特書會于蕭魚者非惡
其厚疑也謂鄭不可信而悼公善勝之績自著
矣吁悼公之於鄭楚經營圖回老成持重雖失
之於前而卒得之於後如此庶幾乎召陵之不
戰而城濮之績不越是矣推原所自又魏絳知
===
武子之力也於乎臣能進言君肯聽言則雖區
區之霸如悼公者功業尚如此而况不為霸者
乎故曰無競維人四方其訓之
城楚丘僖公二年公至自晉昭公十六年
周瑾
同考試官教諭杜批遣詞老健立法森嚴
讀之自能使人懲勸也
考試官教諭姜批作麟經文字有氣可
觀必老手也
punctuated:
之念。由是，兵車百乘，歌鍾二肆，而鄭之賂晉益厚。雖被良霄之執，二十四年之久莫敢叛也。是何遵約束至於許遠耶？良由悼公感之以誠爾。感之以誠，固足以服鄭，而楚人狼貪虎噬之毒自不敢肆矣。是故《春秋》特書「會于蕭魚」者，非惡其厚疑也，謂鄭不可信，而悼公善勝之績自著矣。吁！悼公之於鄭、楚，經營圖回，老成持重，雖失之於前，而卒得之於後如此，庶幾乎召陵之不戰，而城濮之績不越是矣。推原所自，又魏絳、知武子之力也。於乎！臣能進言，君肯聽言，則雖區區之霸如悼公者，功業尚如此，而况不為霸者乎？故曰：「無競維人，四方其訓之。」
城楚丘，僖公二年。公至自晉，昭公十六年。
周瑾
同考試官教諭杜批：遣詞老健，立法森嚴，讀之自能使人懲勸也。
考試官教諭姜批：作麟經文字，有氣可觀，必老手也。
translation_en:
…any thought of suspicion. Thereupon Zheng’s gifts to Jin grew still more lavish: a hundred war chariots and two sets of bells for accompanying song. Even though Liang Xiao was seized, Zheng did not dare rebel for twenty-four years. Why did it abide by the compact for so long? Truly, it was because Duke Dao moved its people through sincerity. Such sincerity was indeed enough to secure Zheng’s submission, while the men of Chu did not dare unleash their venomous rapacity, greedy as wolves and ravenous as tigers. Thus, when the Spring and Autumn Annals specifically records the “meeting at Xiaoyu,” it is not condemning profound suspicion [?]. Rather, it indicates that Zheng could not be trusted, while Duke Dao’s achievement in securing victory by good means becomes manifest of itself.
Ah! In his dealings with Zheng and Chu, Duke Dao planned and maneuvered with seasoned judgment and prudence. Though he erred at first, he ultimately succeeded in this fashion. This came close to the bloodless success at Shaoling, and even the achievement at Chengpu did not surpass it. Tracing this success to its source, we find that it also owed much to Wei Jiang and Zhi Wuzi. Alas! When ministers can offer counsel and their ruler is willing to heed it, even a mere hegemon such as Duke Dao can accomplish so much. How much more, then, can one whose aim goes beyond hegemony! Thus it is said: “Strength lies in worthy men; the four quarters will follow their instruction.”
“Fortification of Chuqiu”—the second year of Duke Xi. “The duke returned from Jin”—the sixteenth year of Duke Zhao.
Zhou Jin.
Comment by Associate Examiner Du, Instructor: His phrasing is seasoned and vigorous, and his compositional method is rigorous. Reading it naturally moves one to take warning and emulate what is good.
Comment by Examiner Jiang, Instructor: In writing on the Classic of the Unicorn [the Spring and Autumn Annals], he displays an impressive vigor. He must be a practiced hand.

title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
考試官教諭張批理明而詞足以發之
作春秋義須如此
奮於自立者春秋之所予甘於自棄者春秋之
所譏此魯昭見辱於晉而安之不及衛文公之
所行多矣春秋備書予奪自見嘗讀易曰天行
健君子以自强不息春秋諸侯知德者鮮矣孰
意衛之文公而亦可語此邪蓋衛為狄滅東徙
渡河野處曹邑被苫蓋蒙荊棘狐狸所居豺狼
所嗥觀許穆夫人載馳之賦蓋有人情所不堪
===
者使文公於此不能振奮而失恐懼省戒之時
則亦後日之魯昭耳胡足取哉文公不然憤悱
警懼恐恐然自强之不暇衣大布之衣服大帛
之冠務材訓農也通商惠工也敬教勸學授方
任能凡所以興滯補弊者筭無遺策卒之元年
革車三十乘季年三百乘而城郭朝市煥然一
新衛之强也日盛矣噫夏少康處微弱之時而
祀夏配天不失舊物文公其庶幾乎春秋於城
楚丘而不書桓公城衛雖曰不與諸侯專封蓋
punctuated:
考試官教諭張批：理明而詞足以發之，作春秋義須如此。

奮於自立者，春秋之所予；甘於自棄者，春秋之所譏。此魯昭見辱於晉而安之，不及衛文公之所行多矣。春秋備書，予奪自見。嘗讀易曰：「天行健，君子以自强不息。」春秋諸侯，知德者鮮矣，孰意衛之文公而亦可語此邪？蓋衛為狄滅，東徙渡河，野處曹邑，被苫蓋，蒙荊棘，狐狸所居，豺狼所嗥。觀許穆夫人載馳之賦，蓋有人情所不堪者。使文公於此不能振奮，而失恐懼省戒之時，則亦後日之魯昭耳，胡足取哉？文公不然，憤悱警懼，恐恐然自强之不暇。衣大布之衣，服大帛之冠，務材訓農也，通商惠工也，敬教勸學，授方任能。凡所以興滯補弊者，筭無遺策。卒之元年革車三十乘，季年三百乘，而城郭朝市煥然一新，衛之强也日盛矣。噫！夏少康處微弱之時，而祀夏配天，不失舊物，文公其庶幾乎？春秋於城楚丘，而不書桓公城衛，雖曰不與諸侯專封，蓋
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Zhang, Instructor: “The reasoning is clear, and the language fully expresses it. This is how an essay interpreting the Spring and Autumn Annals should be written.”

Those who strive to establish themselves earn the approval of the Spring and Autumn Annals; those content to abandon themselves incur its censure. Duke Zhao of Lu accepted humiliation at the hands of Jin complacently, and thus fell far short of Duke Wen of Wei in his conduct. The Spring and Autumn Annals records their deeds fully, and its approval and disapproval become apparent of themselves. I once read in the Book of Changes: “Heaven moves with vigor; the gentleman accordingly strengthens himself without ceasing.” Among the feudal lords of the Spring and Autumn period, few understood virtue. Who would have thought that Duke Wen of Wei, too, could be spoken of in these terms? Wei had been destroyed by the Di. Its people moved east across the Yellow River and lived in the open country at Cao, covering themselves with thatch amid thorns and brambles, where foxes dwelt and jackals and wolves howled. Reading Lady Mu of Xu’s poem “Galloping On” (Zai chi), one finds circumstances that human feelings could scarcely bear.

Had Duke Wen been unable to rouse himself at this juncture, missing the opportunity for fearful reflection and vigilance, he would merely have been another Duke Zhao of Lu in a later age. What would there have been to commend? Duke Wen acted otherwise. Troubled and restless, alert and apprehensive, he anxiously devoted himself to ceaseless self-strengthening. He wore garments of coarse cloth and a cap of plain silk. He fostered useful resources and instructed farmers, facilitated commerce and benefited artisans, honored instruction and encouraged learning, assigned duties and employed the capable. In all that might revive what had languished and remedy defects, his planning left no measure unconsidered. Thus, from thirty war chariots in his first year, he reached three hundred in his final year; the walls, court, and markets were completely renewed, and Wei’s strength grew daily. Ah! Shaokang of Xia lived in a time of weakness and obscurity, yet restored the sacrifices to the Xia ancestors in conjunction with Heaven and preserved the dynasty’s ancient inheritance. Did Duke Wen not come close to this achievement? In recording the walling of Chuqiu, the Spring and Autumn Annals does not state that Duke Huan built walls for Wei. Although this is said to withhold approval from feudal lords who presume to enfeoff on their own authority, presumably …

title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
亦移其善於文公焉耳又甞讀易曰困亨者因
困窮而致亨也魯秉周禮有道者多矣孰意傳
至昭公而獨懵於此耶盖魯為晉辱三見卻於
河上兩拘留於國中足趑趄口囁嚅奔走道途
伺候盟主匪范獻子誘惰之諫必有意料所不
及者使昭公於此耻於危辱而有激昂勉勵之
志則亦前日之衛文耳復何議哉昭公不然淟
涊苟且施施然自得而不耻徒習威儀之末竟
忘守身之本不困心衡慮也不徵色發聲也甘
===
為人下安於辱中凡所以處己待物者舉無成
法卒之今年居于鄆明年次乾侯而辛苦墊隘
無所底告魯之削也滋甚矣噫越句踐當患難
之際而卧薪甞膽志必報吳昭公果知此歟春
秋於公至自晉而不書晉人止公雖曰若為君
父諱辱盖深致其貶於昭公焉耳吁自立也則
小可大弱可强自棄也則强亦弱大亦小春秋
取彼而譏此欲人强於為善之意深切著明矣
抑愚於此又有感焉文公固可予矣齊桓擅天
punctuated:
亦移其善於文公焉耳。又甞讀《易》曰：「困，亨。」者因困窮而致亨也。魯秉周禮，有道者多矣，孰意傳至昭公而獨懵於此耶？盖魯為晉辱，三見卻於河上，兩拘留於國中，足趑趄，口囁嚅，奔走道途，伺候盟主。匪范獻子誘惰之諫，必有意料所不及者。使昭公於此耻於危辱，而有激昂勉勵之志，則亦前日之衛文耳，復何議哉？昭公不然，淟涊苟且，施施然自得而不耻，徒習威儀之末，竟忘守身之本，不困心衡慮也，不徵色發聲也，甘為人下，安於辱中，凡所以處己待物者，舉無成法。卒之今年居于鄆，明年次乾侯，而辛苦墊隘，無所底告，魯之削也滋甚矣。噫！越句踐當患難之際，而卧薪甞膽，志必報吳，昭公果知此歟？《春秋》於「公至自晉」而不書「晉人止公」，雖曰若為君父諱辱，盖深致其貶於昭公焉耳。吁！自立也，則小可大，弱可强；自棄也，則强亦弱，大亦小。《春秋》取彼而譏此，欲人强於為善之意，深切著明矣。
抑愚於此又有感焉：文公固可予矣，齊桓擅天
translation_en:
…it also transfers the credit to Duke Wen. I have also read in the Book of Changes: “Adversity; success.” This means attaining success through hardship and privation. Lu upheld the rites of Zhou and had many men who possessed the Way. Who would have expected that, when the succession reached Duke Zhao, he alone would be oblivious to this? Lu suffered humiliation at Jin’s hands: three times he was turned back at the Yellow River, and twice he was detained within Jin. His feet faltered and his mouth stammered as he hurried along the roads, waiting upon the lord of the covenant. Had it not been for Fan Xianzi’s remonstrance about encouraging laxity [?], something beyond expectation would surely have occurred. Had Duke Zhao felt shame at this peril and humiliation and resolved to rouse himself to greater effort, he would have been another Duke Wen of Wei in earlier days. What further criticism could there have been?
Duke Zhao did otherwise. Mired in disgrace and expediency, he remained complacently self-satisfied and unashamed. He merely practised the superficial details of dignified ceremonial conduct, utterly forgetting the fundamentals of preserving his own person. His heart was not distressed, nor his deliberations thwarted; there was no sign in his countenance or expression in his voice. He willingly submitted to others and rested content in humiliation. In everything concerning his own conduct and his dealings with others, he followed no established standard. In the end, one year he resided at Yun, and the next he lodged at Qianhou, suffering hardship and distress with nowhere to turn for help. Lu’s decline grew ever more severe. Alas! Amid adversity, Goujian of Yue slept on brushwood and tasted gall, determined to avenge himself upon Wu. Did Duke Zhao truly understand this? When the Spring and Autumn Annals records, “The duke returned from Jin,” without recording, “The men of Jin detained the duke,” it may seem to conceal humiliation on behalf of one’s ruler and father, but in fact it directs profound censure at Duke Zhao.
Ah! Through self-reliance, the small can become great and the weak strong; through self-abandonment, even the strong become weak and the great small. In approving the former and censuring the latter, the Spring and Autumn Annals makes its intention—that people should exert themselves in doing good—profoundly earnest and manifestly clear.
Yet I, in my humble opinion, have a further reflection on this. Duke Wen certainly deserves approval, but Duke Huan of Qi usurped the Son of Heaven’s …

Although this seemed to restore a fallen state and continue an extinguished ruling line, how did it accord with the system for enfeoffing states in the Offices of Zhou? Duke Zhao certainly deserves criticism. Yet Duke Zhao of Jin listened to the accusations of the people of Ju and rebuffed Lu. Although this seemed to restrain the strong and support the weak, how did it accord with Confucius’s teaching on discernment and far-sightedness? Alas! Was this why Duke Huan advanced no further than hegemony, while Duke Zhao of Jin suffered declining power and failed to rise? The Doctrine of the Mean prizes rejecting slander. There is good reason why the gentleman esteems discussion of the Kingly Way.

Record of Rites

“In ordering ranks at court, governing armies, administering offices, and enforcing laws, authority and dignity cannot take effect without ritual propriety.”

Zheng Wan

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Instructor: “His exposition of how these four activities must depend upon ritual propriety displays abundant coherence and insight. Moreover, his style is lucid and vigorous, far beyond the reach of the other compositions. For these reasons it is selected.”

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Instructor: “Thorough in his grasp of principle and refined in his diction. Who but you could rank first in this examining section?”

Thus, at court, positions are higher and lower; unless their ranks are ordered, court ceremonial will lack regularity. One must ensure that dukes and ministers are ranked …

title: 正德八年廣西鄉試錄
text:
上大夫士序于下等級分明井乎其不紊軍旅
之事局有左右不治則軍容不飭矣必使旣樹
和門於左又樹和門於右部分嚴明森乎其難
越若夫分職以涖官貴得其體也如天官掌邦
治地官掌邦敎俾凡次于朝著靖共爾位可
焉謹守以行法貴得其施也如施典于邦國施
則于都鄙俾凡隸于官司者恪遵成憲可焉然
治此庶政而欲威嚴之行舍禮其何以耶盖禮
以剛斷為主截然而不可易所以服人心者在
===
是以裁割為義凛然而不可踰所以定民志者
在是如班朝也治軍也不以禮為綱維吾見尊
卑之體統不明監領之紀律不整人將輕於犯
違可慢而不可畏矣威嚴其能以自行乎威嚴
之不行政之不行也禮可忽於斯哉如涖官也
行法也不以禮為防範吾見百司之職業不脩
一王之貞度不振人將易於抗背知玩而不知
憚矣威嚴其能以自行乎威嚴之不行政之不
行也禮可離於斯哉吁治政必待於禮而後行
punctuated: 上，大夫士序于下，等級分明，井乎其不紊。軍旅之事，局有左右，不治則軍容不飭矣。必使旣樹和門於左，又樹和門於右，部分嚴明，森乎其難越。若夫分職以涖官，貴得其體也。如天官掌邦治，地官掌邦敎，俾凡次于朝著，靖共爾位，可焉。謹守以行法，貴得其施也。如施典于邦國，施則于都鄙，俾凡隸于官司者恪遵成憲，可焉。然治此庶政，而欲威嚴之行，舍禮其何以耶？盖禮以剛斷為主，截然而不可易，所以服人心者在是；以裁割為義，凛然而不可踰，所以定民志者在是。如班朝也，治軍也，不以禮為綱維，吾見尊卑之體統不明，監領之紀律不整，人將輕於犯違，可慢而不可畏矣。威嚴其能以自行乎？威嚴之不行，政之不行也。禮可忽於斯哉？如涖官也，行法也，不以禮為防範，吾見百司之職業不脩，一王之貞度不振，人將易於抗背，知玩而不知憚矣。威嚴其能以自行乎？威嚴之不行，政之不行也。禮可離於斯哉？吁！治政必待於禮而後行。
translation_en:
…above, with grand masters and servicemen ranked below, so that distinctions of rank are clear and everything is orderly and free of confusion. In military affairs, positions are assigned to the left and right; without proper ordering, military formations will lack discipline. Gates of Harmony must be erected both on the left and on the right, so that the divisions of the troops are strictly defined and imposing in their inviolability. As for allocating duties in administering offices, what matters is achieving the proper organization. For example, the Officials of Heaven oversee the governance of the realm, and the Officials of Earth oversee its instruction: it will suffice to ensure that all who hold positions at court attend respectfully to their stations. In carefully maintaining the implementation of laws, what matters is their proper application. For example, applying the statutes to the feudal states and the regulations to the metropolitan and outlying domains will suffice, provided that all who belong to government offices scrupulously observe established laws. Yet in administering these many affairs, how can one make commanding authority effective without ritual propriety? Ritual propriety takes firmness and decisiveness as its governing principle: its distinctions are clear-cut and cannot be altered. This is how it wins the submission of people’s hearts. It takes discrimination and delimitation as its essential meaning: it is awe-inspiring and cannot be transgressed. This is how it settles the people’s purposes.

In arranging ranks at court and governing the army, unless ritual propriety provides the guiding framework, I foresee that the hierarchical order of superior and inferior will become unclear and the disciplinary rules of command will fall into disorder. People will then readily commit violations; authority will invite contempt rather than fear. Can commanding authority take effect of itself? When commanding authority fails to take effect, government fails to take effect. Can ritual propriety be neglected here? In administering offices and implementing laws, unless ritual propriety supplies restraints, I foresee that the duties of the various offices will go unfulfilled and the enduring standards of sovereign rule will cease to be upheld. People will then readily resist and disobey, knowing only how to make light of authority, without knowing how to fear it. Can commanding authority take effect of itself? When commanding authority fails to take effect, government fails to take effect. Can ritual propriety be dispensed with here? Ah! The administration of government must depend upon ritual propriety before it can take effect…
